segment_name: The Fog and the System: Opening into Chancery

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-chat that stuck with me — that the tragedy of this opening isn't really Chancery's fault, it's people's *silence* that feeds the machine. That feels almost counter-intuitive given how much Dickens is attacking the legal system. Can you make that case?
questions.intent: Get Caroline's strongest take on silence as the real engine of tragedy, setting up immediate tension with Blackstone's institutional violence reading

questions.question: James, you're already shaking your head — because I think you'd say that framing puts the blame on the victims. That dead man in the coffin passage, the one with 'no more track behind him than a deserted infant' — was he silent by choice, or did the system just make him illegible?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement with Caroline, get Blackstone to read the coffin passage, and force the question of agency vs. structure into the open

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in on the technique here, because you'd say both James and Caroline are actually arguing *about* Dickens's content — and missing that the *form* is doing something stranger. You mentioned the nesting of voices in the Jarndyce passage, Lady Dedlock's sister 'dying' to him buried inside reported speech inside a recounting. What is that construction actually doing to us as readers?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's formalist argument about narrative structure mirroring Chancery, and get her to read the nested passage — creating a third angle that reframes the James/Caroline debate

questions.question: Caroline, Eleanor just said the fog isn't natural — it's Dickens's architectural choice, a designed experience. But you've pushed back on that kind of reading before. Does calling it 'artifice' risk making it cold? Because Mrs. Rouncewell's 'My Lady, you must have a heart to pity me' — that doesn't feel constructed. That feels like someone just *breaking*.
questions.intent: Set up the realism-vs-artifice clash between Caroline and Eleanor, get Caroline to read the Rouncewell plea, and test whether emotional directness and formal design can coexist

questions.question: James, you said you'd probably get angry during this conversation — and I want to hold you to that. If Dickens is showing us a system that traps even the people running it, lawyers, judges, Lady Dedlock herself, then what exactly are we supposed to *do* with that? Is this novel a diagnosis or is it a counsel of despair?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone toward his most politically urgent argument, create a moment of genuine heat, and open up the question of whether Bleak House offers any way out — which both Eleanor and Caroline will want to contest

steering_notes: The real fault line in this segment is between Blackstone's structural-institutional reading, Caroline's psychological-agency reading, and Eleanor's formalist reading. Don't let any two of them settle into agreement too quickly — all three positions are genuinely incompatible at their edges. The coffin passage is the shared text everyone wants to quote, so use it as a pivot: ask each expert what *kind* of violence it's depicting. Keep the energy on the word 'silence' — it means something different to each of them and the collision is productive. If the conversation gets too abstract, pull it back to Mrs. Rouncewell's plea, which is the most viscerally human moment and the one most likely to generate real disagreement about whether Dickens earns his emotional effects.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline says silence feeds Chancery; James says silence is the *rational response* to Chancery — these are directly incompatible and should be forced into direct contact early
Eleanor's claim that 'the form IS the argument' directly challenges both James's thematic reading and Caroline's emotional realism reading — she should be asked to respond to each of them by name

James and Caroline both want to quote 'died to him' but for opposite reasons: James reads it as institutional death, Caroline reads it as self-imposed noble erasure driven by pride — this is a perfect close-reading collision

Eleanor's point about Mrs. Rouncewell's syntax mirroring silence will likely frustrate Caroline, who reads the same line as Dickens breaking through artifice into directness — get them to read the line aloud and disagree about what they're hearing

segment_name: The Weight of Narrative Layers: How Dickens Builds Unreliability

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that every purple passage in this novel is 'both genuinely moving and a con.' Can you take us to that moment in chapter eleven, the lament over the dead man, 'where is she, while these ashes are above the ground' — and show us what you mean? Because on the page it feels sincere. Where does the con happen?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to perform the seduction-and-betrayal of Dickens's sentiment aloud, setting up the core tension of the segment and establishing her formal argument before others can respond

questions.question: James, I think you're going to disagree with that framing. Because you told me the narrator's lament there isn't a con — it's actually a critique of sympathy itself, Dickens admitting he doesn't know who this man was or what he needed. Is that the same thing Caroline's saying, or is that a completely different argument?
questions.intent: Provoke direct engagement between James and Caroline on whether Dickens's sentiment is self-aware manipulation or institutional critique — surface the distinction between formal and political readings

questions.question: Eleanor, you've both been circling around this chapter twelve passage — 'whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation' — and I want you to read it for us, because you told me the syntax itself *does* something. What is it actually doing on a sentence level? And does it matter whether we're talking about Tulkinghorn's power or Dickens's narrative architecture — or are those the same thing?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to quote and perform c12:p116, then pivot to her structural argument about form-as-content, which should create friction with both James's institutional reading and Caroline's musical-prose reading

questions.question: Okay James, you've been sitting on this — because Eleanor just called that passage narrative architecture, and you've told me it's really about how Victorian power actually worked, asymmetric information, the threat of exposure. Are those compatible readings, or is one of them letting Dickens off the hook for something?
questions.intent: Force the political vs. aesthetic tension into the open — is calling it 'architecture' a way of aestheticizing what is actually a description of coercion? Get James's sharpest institutional argument against the literary readings

questions.question: I want to end on Richard Carstone, because all three of you flagged him and you all seem to disagree. Eleanor, you said his confession to Esther — 'I wish I were more constant' — shows self-awareness that changes nothing, which you think proves Dickens's point about omniscience being a trap. James thinks Richard is just performing his own failure. Caroline thinks the awkwardness IS the truth of his character. Who's right — and does it matter that we're hearing this through Esther, who has every reason to want him to be okay?
questions.intent: Force a three-way collision on c23:p37 using the Esther-as-narrator problem as the wedge — pull together the unreliability question, the question of character sympathy, and the question of whether knowing more helps you at all

steering_notes: The segment's energy should feel like three people who've all read the same book and arrived at completely different novels. Don't let anyone stay purely abstract — push for passages read aloud whenever possible, especially c12:p116 and c22:p51. Caroline is the one most likely to make this feel alive and musical; Eleanor will give you the architecture; James will keep everyone honest about what the novel is actually *for*. The risk is that Eleanor and James agree too quickly on unreliability-as-structure and leave Caroline's formal argument unheard — watch for that and triangulate. The Richard Carstone question should feel like an ambush: they'll all think they agree until they realize they don't.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues form-becomes-content (c12:p116 syntax mirrors obsessive surveillance) while Caroline argues the same passage is about prose music and withheld information — they may sound like they agree but they're describing completely different mechanisms; push on this

James's reading of the narrator's lament (c11:p92) as a critique of sympathy directly contradicts Caroline's reading of it as deliberate excess — this should produce real disagreement about whether Dickens is in control of his sentimentality or subject to it

James dismisses Richard's confession as self-pitying performance while Eleanor calls it proof that self-knowledge changes nothing — these are actually compatible but they don't know it yet; the Esther question is what separates them

Caroline and Eleanor both resist moralizing readings but for opposite reasons: Caroline because the unreliability is formal, Eleanor because omniscience is a trap — get them to argue about whether that difference matters

questions.question: James, you said before we started that Richard's real crime is *believing* the system is fair—that he actually takes Jarndyce's advice seriously. But doesn't that let Richard off the hook a bit? I mean, lots of people believe the system is fair and don't collapse the way he does. What's Dickens actually showing us here—systemic failure, or something more specific to Richard?
questions.intent: Open the central disagreement: institutional tragedy vs. character tragedy. Get Blackstone to commit hard to the systemic reading before Eleanor and Caroline push back.

questions.question: Eleanor, I want you to read that passage at c13:p124—the sunlight one, the 'burst of light' moment. Because you described it as 'architecturally precise' rather than metaphorical. What do you mean by that? What's the difference, and why does it matter for how we read Richard's whole arc?
questions.intent: Get the c13:p124 passage read aloud and establish Eleanor's structural-prophecy argument. Sets up Blackstone's counter that the shadow is literal institutional darkness, not formal elegance.

questions.question: Caroline, you said Jarndyce is eloquent *because* he's helpless—that his wisdom becomes almost complicit in the delusion it's warning against. That's a really uncomfortable idea. Can you take us to that passage at c13:p118, the heathen waggoner bit, and show us exactly where you hear that helplessness in the prose? Because on the surface it sounds like perfectly good advice.
questions.intent: Get c13:p118 read aloud and surface the irony that Jarndyce's sermon plants the seeds of Richard's failure. Creates a three-way tension: Eleanor sees structural doom, Blackstone sees class blindness, Caroline hears rhetorical impotence.

questions.question: Eleanor, I have to push you on something. You said Esther's narration at c13:p99—the bit where she literally places herself between Richard and Ada—is 'doing something brilliant' by showing complicity. But James is basically arguing the whole novel is complicit in blaming the individual when it should be blaming Chancery. Are those two kinds of complicity the same thing, or is Dickens playing a double game here?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Eleanor's formal-complicity reading and Blackstone's ideological-complicity reading. The word 'complicit' should bounce productively between all three experts.

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Caroline, you said the real horror is that everyone in these passages *knows better and says the right things and it changes nothing*. If that's true—if being right and eloquent saves no one—then what exactly is Dickens asking us to do with a novel that's full of right, eloquent people? Is Bleak House pessimistic about its own power to mean anything?
questions.intent: Pull back to the big question about the novel's purpose and whether Dickens believes in his own moral architecture. Designed to produce genuine disagreement about whether the book is tragic, nihilistic, or something else entirely.

steering_notes: The session has a natural three-way tension that should run the whole segment: Eleanor sees formal/architectural tragedy, Blackstone sees institutional critique, Caroline sees rhetorical impotence. Don't let any one frame dominate too early. Push back when anyone sounds too settled. The word 'complicit' appears in all three pre-interviews and should be surfaced explicitly—it's the live wire connecting all their readings. Prioritise getting at least two passages read aloud (c13:p124 and c13:p118); the Mrs. Badger passage at c17:p19 can come in naturally if Blackstone pushes the class-anxiety angle. Keep energy informal—this is a disagreement between smart people who've all read carefully, not a seminar.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone argues Jarndyce's Providence-and-effort advice is class-blind fantasy; Eleanor argues Jarndyce already *knows* it won't work and is performing rather than counseling—these are different accusations against the same speech and should collide directly

Caroline says Richard lacks internal friction and the tragedy is internal before external; Blackstone says the tragedy is institutional before personal—this is a direct contradiction about causality and should be named as such

All three experts want to quote c13:p124 but for completely different reasons: Eleanor sees formal prophecy, Blackstone sees the novel's admission that hope is the trap, Caroline sees Dickens's own ambivalence about youth. Reading it once and then asking what each of them hears could be a strong single moment

Caroline's claim that Jarndyce is complicit in the delusion he's warning against directly echoes Eleanor's claim about Esther at c13:p99—draw the parallel explicitly and ask whether the whole novel is structured around well-meaning complicity

segment_name: Secrets and Shame: Lady Dedlock's Impossible Position

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that Lady Dedlock discovers her own past *through Sir Leicester's words*. She doesn't confess, she doesn't choose, she just... overhears her own exposure. Can you walk us through that moment in c12:p11? What does the prose actually sound like when her world collapses?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read or closely paraphrase the 'I have seen him' passage and establish her core argument about narrative agency before the others can frame it their way

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on that. Because you'd say — and tell me if I'm wrong — that this isn't really about Lady Dedlock's psychology at all. It's about the *shape* of the novel. She's trapped not by guilt but by the fact that Dickens has built a machine that keeps her perpetually about to be discovered. Is that fair? And does that mean we're supposed to feel complicit in her exposure?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to articulate her structural-voyeurism argument and set up a direct clash with Woodcourt's agency reading and Blackstone's institutional one

questions.question: James, you'd say both of them are still too focused on Lady Dedlock herself — and that the real story is Tulkinghorn. That he's not a villain exactly, he's more like... a bureaucrat with a dossier. What does it mean that the person who destroys her isn't motivated by hatred or desire, just by this cold administrative *legibility*? Is that more frightening than a proper antagonist?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's surveillance-capitalism reading and his argument that institutional exposure is more damning than personal malice — should provoke Hartley on structure vs. system and Woodcourt on agency

questions.question: Let's bring in Jo for a second, because all three of you want to quote him — 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!' from c11:p88. Caroline, you connect that to what Lady Dedlock's world has *destroyed*. James sees it as evidence of institutional obscenity. Eleanor thinks the grammar itself is doing the emotional work. Can you make the case that Jo and Lady Dedlock are actually in the same trap — or are they so far apart socially that comparing them is almost obscene in itself?
questions.intent: Force a three-way confrontation over the Jo passage and whether class proximity or distance is the point — should surface Blackstone's systemic reading against Hartley's formalist one

questions.question: Last one, and I want to end on a fight if we can get one. Eleanor, you think the name 'Bleak House' at c64:p27 is a structural joke — irony embedded in the architecture, not comfort. James, I suspect, thinks it's Dickens letting sentiment off the hook. Caroline, you're somewhere in the middle on Ada's child as either redemption or delusion. So: does this novel actually believe in repair? Or is the ending — the name, the baby, the restored house — Dickens writing a happy ending he doesn't quite trust himself?
questions.intent: Provoke a three-way disagreement about whether the novel's resolution is genuinely hopeful, formally ironic, or sentimentally evasive — get all three competing readings into direct collision for the close of the segment

steering_notes: The key tension to keep live throughout is structural vs. institutional vs. psychological — Hartley thinks the form is the argument, Blackstone thinks the system is the villain, Woodcourt thinks the human experience of powerlessness is the point. Don't let any one frame dominate too early. The Jo passage (c11:p88) is a good reset button if the conversation gets too abstract — it's concrete, emotional, and all three experts have strong but different readings of it. Push for actual quotation where possible: 'I have seen him' and the unfinished house passage from c23:p41 are the two most generative. Watch for Blackstone and Hartley talking past each other on 'structural' — they mean completely different things by it and that confusion could be productive or a dead end depending on when it surfaces.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that Lady Dedlock is trapped by *narrative form* directly contradicts Woodcourt's claim that she's trapped by *someone else's authority to tell her story* — these sound similar but are fundamentally different arguments about where the power lives, and they should be asked to address each other directly

Blackstone's reading of Ada's redemption fantasy as sentiment doing the work repeal should do is a direct provocation to Woodcourt's more sympathetic reading of the same passage (c60:p123) — this is the clearest disagreement in the pre-interviews and should be surfaced explicitly

All three experts want to quote Jo (c11:p88) but for incompatible reasons: Hartley for the *form* of grief, Woodcourt for the *presence* of feeling, Blackstone for the *obscenity* of his later destruction — asking them to account for each other's reading of the same four words should generate real friction

Blackstone's Tulkinghorn-as-bureaucrat argument is implicitly a challenge to Hartley's auteur-Dickens argument: if the structure makes us voyeurs, who built the structure? Dickens or the legal system he's depicting? That's a genuine philosophical disagreement worth surfacing mid-segment

segment_name: The Child and the City: Jo's Testimony Against Society

questions.question: Eleanor, you've said that Dickens doesn't just *complain* about the legal system—he replaces it with something else entirely. Can you read us that line from c11:p100, the 'distant ray of light' bit, and explain what you mean by narrative authority? Because that's a big claim.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the apostrophe passage aloud and articulate her strongest take—that the narrator performs a counter-legal act—before Blackstone can reframe it as mere sentiment

questions.question: James, you heard Eleanor. She's saying Dickens solves the problem through storytelling. But your argument is much colder—you're saying the law isn't *failing* Jo, it's succeeding at exactly what it was designed to do. Does it matter that Dickens found a literary workaround if the actual system rolls on unchanged?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's structural critique and Hartley's formal/literary argument—is narrative authority a real counter-power or an aesthetic consolation prize?

questions.question: Caroline, both James and Eleanor are treating Jo as a kind of test case—for the legal system, for narrative form. But you've said he's also just a *character*, and there's something the other readings might be steamrolling. When you read 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'—what's actually happening there that gets lost if we treat it purely as a political argument?
questions.intent: Draw out Caroline's insistence on Jo's interiority and emotional texture, and set up the tension with Hartley's formal reading and Blackstone's structural one—does caring about Jo as a person change the argument?

questions.question: James, you want to defend Vholes—you've said he's not a villain, he's just rational. But Caroline's asked whether he even belongs in this conversation about Jo. So make the case: why does 'that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth' belong in the same breath as 'no father, no mother, no friends'?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to connect his Vholes reading to Jo's testimony rather than letting it sit as a separate critique—and invite Caroline to push back on whether it muddies the emotional register of the segment

questions.question: Last one, and I want everyone in on this. Eleanor, you've said the fragmented syntax of c11:p78—'Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on.'—is a formal choice, not just realism. Caroline thinks it's also about character. James thinks the form doesn't matter if the structure of the law doesn't change. So who's right? Is Dickens's real weapon the sentence, the system, or the reader?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or collision on the central question of the segment—where does Dickens actually locate his moral and political authority, and does it matter?

steering_notes: The big tension to manage is between Blackstone's structural/legal reading and Hartley's formal/literary one—they agree on the diagnosis but sharply disagree on what Dickens is *doing* about it. Let that run. Caroline is the wild card who humanizes both arguments and should be used to ground abstract claims back in the actual prose whenever the conversation gets too theoretical. Don't let Blackstone colonize the Vholes material too early—save it for question four so it lands as a deliberate provocation rather than a tangent. The goal is to get all three of them arguing about the same three lines from slightly different angles by the end.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's 'narrative authority replaces the law' claim directly contradicts Blackstone's implicit skepticism that aesthetic solutions change systemic problems—surface this explicitly in Q2

Blackstone's insistence that Jo's exclusion is the law *working as designed* vs. Woodcourt's claim that society has already rejected Jo before the law gets involved—these are compatible but the emphasis differs enough to generate friction

Hartley's reading of the fragmented syntax as formal craft vs. Woodcourt's reading of it as character psychology—both quote the same passage (c11:p78) but for opposite reasons; get them to read it against each other in Q5

Woodcourt's skepticism about Vholes belonging in this segment (c39:p4) is a direct invitation for Blackstone to defend his framing—use Q4 to surface this rather than let it sit as a background disagreement

segment_name: Laughter in the Darkness: Dickens's Comic Relief and Moral Purpose

questions.question: Caroline, I want to start with the very first page of the novel — the Megalosaurus waddling up Holborn Hill. Read it to us if you would. Because I think there's a question lurking there about what kind of laugh that is. Is it actually funny? Or is it something weirder than that?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read passage c1:p0 aloud and articulate her 'apocalyptic comedy' thesis — sets up the core tension of the segment immediately

questions.question: Eleanor, let's get into the Mrs. Snagsby shadow passage — c25:p58. You said the repetition there is 'doing work.' Can you read it and actually show us what you mean? Because I want to hear where the joke ends and the horror starts — if they even do separate.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read and close-read the shadow passage, demonstrating her 'structural engine' thesis — positions her slightly differently from Caroline who sees it as verbal music versus Eleanor who sees it as architectural

questions.question: James, I'm going to push you on something. Both Caroline and Eleanor are basically saying the comedy and the darkness are fused — you can't separate them. But you said something in our chat that felt different to me: that the Smallweed passage, Bucket's line about the family selling each other for a pound or two, is 'not funny.' Full stop. So are you actually disagreeing with them? Is there a point where Dickens stops making you laugh and just makes you feel sick?
questions.intent: Surface Blackstone's distinction between comedy-as-critique and passages that have crossed into something colder — provoke disagreement with Caroline and Eleanor who both insist on the fused laugh-and-horror effect

questions.question: James, you said something that I keep coming back to — that the tradespeople managing Lady Dedlock aren't really characters with inner lives, they're nodes in a network. Eleanor, you're nodding, but I suspect you disagree. Doesn't that reading actually strip out exactly the kind of moral complexity you're both saying the comedy creates?
questions.intent: Directly engineer a disagreement between Blackstone's systemic-nodes reading and Eleanor's view that the comic doubling creates moral visibility of individual suffering — also tests Caroline's position on minor characters as 'fully realized'

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Caroline, you said laughing at the Smallweed family makes us complicit. James says it's an indictment of capitalism dissolving human bonds. Eleanor says it's a microcosm of Chancery. Those can't all be true at once — or can they? What is Dickens actually asking us to do when we laugh at these people?
questions.intent: Force a synthesis or a genuine three-way disagreement about the ultimate moral function of the comedy — good closing energy, lets each expert stake out final ground

steering_notes: The big fault line to exploit: James wants to insist some passages have crossed out of comedy entirely into cold indictment, while Caroline and Eleanor both insist the laugh and the horror are always fused. Push James on this distinction early and keep returning to it. Also watch for the characters-vs-systems tension between James (nodes in a network) and Eleanor (moral visibility through doubling) — that could run hot. Caroline's verbal-music angle is the most accessible entry point for listeners, so open there, but don't let it dominate; steer toward the harder moral questions by the midpoint. If energy dips, ask someone to read aloud — all three have strong passages queued up and reading changes the room temperature immediately.
cross_engagement_targets: James says the Smallweed passage 'is not funny — it's terrifying dressed as comedy' while Caroline and Eleanor both insist the laugh and the moral horror are inseparable and simultaneous — this is a genuine disagreement about whether Dickens ever lets the comic mask drop entirely

Eleanor's 'structural engine' reading of the Mrs. Snagsby repetition and Caroline's 'verbal music' reading cover the same passage with different emphases — get them to debate whether it matters if the effect is architectural or aesthetic

James's claim that the tradespeople are 'nodes in a network, not characters with rich interiority' cuts directly against Caroline's insistence that the minor characters 'deserve our attention as fully realized comic creations' — surface this explicitly

segment_name: The Web Tightens: Convergence and Consequences

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started that some of this novel only fully lands when you hear it out loud. So let's test that — can you actually read us the 'whether' passage from chapter 12? And then tell me: what does hearing it do that reading it on the page doesn't?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to perform c12:p114 aloud, establishing the passage as the segment's centrepiece and priming the others to respond to it from their own angles

questions.question: Eleanor, you called that passage — the one we just heard — the grammar of psychological suspense. But James, I know you've got a different read on it. Eleanor, go first: what's Dickens actually doing there, architecturally?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's structural-epistemic reading of c12:p114 as a three-way knowledge trap, setting up direct collision with Blackstone's institutional-power reading

questions.question: James, Eleanor just used the word 'trap' — but she means something almost aesthetic by it, a reader trapped in uncertainty. You'd say there's a much more literal trap operating here, wouldn't you? Because Tulkinghorn isn't mysterious to you at all.
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone into his hardest-edged take — Tulkinghorn as blackmail technician, Lady Dedlock's silence as legal coercion — and force a direct confrontation with Eleanor's 'moral opacity' argument

questions.question: Caroline, James just said Lady Dedlock's silence isn't nobility or psychological depth — it's coercion, she's legally mute. But in chapter 12 you also said Tulkinghorn is almost *pitiable*. James clearly thinks that's romanticizing a predator. Are you actually disagreeing about the novel, or about whether Dickens *wants* us to feel sympathy for people doing terrible things to each other?
questions.intent: Surface the core disagreement between Caroline and Blackstone — tragic dignity vs. moral flatness — and force Caroline to defend her reading of Tulkinghorn's opacity against Blackstone's functional villain argument

questions.question: Eleanor, you brought up George's walk through Chesney Wold — 'blank, blank as the darkness above and below' — and said it was almost Beckettian. That's a big claim for a Victorian novel. What do you mean by that, and does it change anything about how we read the rest of this segment?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to quote and unpack c58:p98, opening the segment out beyond Tulkinghorn to the wider architecture of entrapment; also lets Caroline respond on the prose rhythm and James on the institutional loneliness of characters the law has hollowed out

steering_notes: The c12:p114 passage should anchor the whole segment — get it read aloud early via Caroline and then let each expert fight over what it means. The core productive tension is between Eleanor's aesthetic-structural reading (Dickens as architect of uncertainty), Blackstone's materialist reading (Dickens as anatomist of institutional power), and Caroline's affective-performative reading (Dickens as psychologist of exhaustion). Don't let them talk past each other by using different vocabularies — if Eleanor says 'epistemic trap' and James says 'coercion,' push them to say whether those are the same thing. The Tulkinghorn-as-pitiable vs. Tulkinghorn-as-predator argument is the segment's best fight: keep returning to it. Let the George passage land near the end as an emotional gear-change — it opens the novel's emotional logic outward just as the conversation risks becoming too abstract.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues Tulkinghorn's power comes from moral opacity; Blackstone explicitly rejects mystifying him as a 'technician of blackmail dressed as a gentleman' — push them to say whether opacity and functionality are actually incompatible

Caroline says Lady Dedlock's silence is about psychological exhaustion; Blackstone says it's about legal imprisonment — these are not obviously contradictory and could productively collapse into each other if pushed

Eleanor and Caroline both want to quote c12:p114 and c58:p98 but for completely different reasons (structure vs. sound) — let them each read a phrase and explain why *that* word or rhythm matters, which will make the disagreement concrete rather than theoretical

Blackstone's claim that 'we haven't fixed this, we've just changed who holds the secrets' is the segment's sharpest contemporary hook — save it for a moment when the conversation risks feeling purely historical
